title: 小模型的结构化输出：语法如何确保每个 JSON 答案都有效，以及它无法修复的一个错误
author: AI Explore
content:
Part 8 of ten. Each post is a short, plain-words tour of one lesson from e=mc², a free build-an-LLM-from-scratch course; the full lesson, notebook and numbers are on the site.

A language model that only talks is a toy; the moment it has to fill in a form that a program will run, it becomes a tool, and that is exactly where it starts to break. Yesterday's post left you a tiny model that could read a question and name the right operation to run. That is half a decision. Today the same model fills in the other half, which metric, which territory, which month, how many, as JSON a program can execute with nobody in between. I want to show you the one trick that makes every answer valid, and the one number that trick cannot touch.

The form at the counter

Picture Momo, the monkey, working at a message post with seven counters. Each counter does one job, and each needs its own form filled in first. One counter ranks a metric; its form wants a metric from a list of ten, a level, and optionally a count, a direction, a territory code like T-123, a product and a month. Each box on the form is a slot. The filled-in form is JSON: a short text of keys and values, the way programs like to be told things.

Momo has 0.84 million parameters, small enough to answer in six milliseconds on an ordinary CPU, and small enough to make small mistakes. Writing freely, he gets a lot right and then adds a box the form does not have, or forgets to close the final brace. The counter rejects the whole form.

Ella's stencil

Ella, the elephant, is the teacher. Tonight she holds a stencil over Momo's pen.

This is constrained decoding. A model writes one token at a time, with a scored list of guesses before each. Ella looks at what Momo has written so far and asks of every possible next token: could this still be finished into a form the counter accepts? Every token that could not is masked out before Momo picks. He still chooses, but only among tokens that keep the form alive.

The stencil is a grammar, and the question it asks is called prefix validity. Nobody hand-wrote this grammar; it is built from the catalog that the real project, pankhllm, already keeps: which operations exist, which parameters each takes and in what order, which words each pick-list allows, what shape a code or a month must have, what range a number must fall in. Momo cannot write a parameter the operation lacks, skip a required one, or close the brace too early.

One lovely detail. Momo has a vocabulary of words, so he cannot reliably spell a code like T-412. Instead he writes a pointer, in effect "the first code in the question", and Ella copies the real characters in afterwards.

The whole stencil is a Python function called once per token. Condensed, it fits on a card: 

# condensed from the notebook's value_options and decode
def value_options(spec, ctx): # legal tokens after a parameter name
 if spec["type"] == "enum": # listed words (grounded: only ones the question names)
 return {f'"{v}"' for v in spec["values"] if not ctx["grounded"] or named_in(ctx["q"], v, spec)}
 if spec["type"] == "string": # markers whose real value fits the pattern
 return {m for m, v in ctx["vals"].items() if re.fullmatch(spec["pattern"], v)}
 if spec["type"] == "integer": # number markers inside the range
 return {m for m, v in ctx["vals"].items() if v.isdigit() and spec["min"] <= int(v) <= spec["max"]}

logits = logits + mask(allowed_next(ctx, written_so_far)) # -inf everywhere else, then argmax

On the site, a widget steps through it: three questions, token by token, Momo's top guesses on one side and what the stencil allowed on the other.

Two stencils, one extra rule

The lesson builds two. The catalog stencil enforces everything the catalog says about shape. The grounded stencil adds one rule: a pick-list word is allowed only if that word, or a known alias of it, appears in the question. If nobody mentioned a product, Momo cannot add one. The aliases come from the catalog too; "total scripts" means one metric, "YoY" means a comparison to the prior year.

That one rule turns out to be the whole story.

The numbers, honestly

One run, 11 October 2026, on an Apple Silicon Mac with the GPU shared with other jobs; the whole notebook took 96.5 seconds. The test is 2,000 questions from templates the model never trained on, always taking the top token.

  • Free decoding, no stencil: 91.6% valid JSON. 47.3% exactly right, operation and every parameter. 44.4% valid but wrong. Operation alone right 84.5% of the time. The failures were near-misses: an extra parameter on an operation that has none, and 43 outputs that did not even parse.
  • Catalog stencil: validity 100.0%. Exact match barely moved, 47.3% to 50.5%, and the operation was right 84.5% of the time, exactly as before. The invalid answers did not become right; they became valid wrong ones, 49.5%.
  • Grounded stencil: validity 100.0%, exact match 71.3%, wrong but valid 28.7%, operation right 90.8%. Momo could no longer name a product nobody asked about.
  • Speed: a full JSON answer took 6.0 milliseconds at the median on the CPU, about 11 tokens. The operation alone, 0.87 milliseconds.

Of the 574 wrong-but-valid answers left, 390 had the right operation with one parameter wrong or missing, often a dropped "bottom", and 184 had the wrong operation outright.

Here is the idea I most want you to leave with. A grammar guarantees the format and nothing about the meaning. The catalog stencil proves it: validity jumped to 100% and the number of right answers hardly changed, because every answer that used to fail loudly now failed quietly, as a perfectly shaped form filled in wrongly.

That quiet failure is the dangerous one. A program will happily run a valid, wrong request. So the number to watch is wrong but valid, not "how often is the output valid". Grounding helped because it is the one part of the stencil that checks the answer against the question: a check on meaning, not on shape. Hosted "JSON mode" features in big APIs are the same idea with a bigger grammar, and the same limit.

The confidence score carries the same lesson. With the grounded stencil, a fixed threshold let the model decide 72.1% of the questions at 98.54% precision. An earlier run of the same notebook gave 93.49% at that threshold, so I do not lean on it. On 14 questions written for a different catalog, the operation was right on 11, and one miss was the bad kind:

Why did calls fall in T-112 in 2026-08?

The model sent that to the counter that reports a KPI's value, with a confidence of 0.996. Valid, confident, and wrong. The next lesson replaces that confidence with something sturdier.

What you can take from this

If you ever ask a model for JSON, do two things. Constrain the decoding; it is a short function and it turns the format from a hope into a guarantee. Then measure the error that still parses, because that is the one the grammar hides. The three-way results table, the condensed stencil and the notebook that rebuilds all 22,000 questions byte for byte before training are all on the site.

Want to actually build it?

This post is the postcard. The lesson is the trip. Lesson 08 of e=mc² on theaivibe.org walks you through every piece with widgets you can poke, a notebook that runs on a free GPU in minutes, and the honest numbers at every step. No account, no paywall, nothing to install.

  • Start here: https://theaivibe.org/emc2/structured-output-small-model-json-constrained-decoding
  • The whole ten-lesson journey: https://theaivibe.org/emc2

Tomorrow, Lesson 09 leaves templates behind: a bigger model labels real human phrasings, and three small models, today's among them, learn from 183 of its own decisions.
aiSummary: 文章展示了如何通过语法模板进行受约束解码，确保小模型输出的 JSON 100% 有效，同时指出仅保证格式并不能避免那些仍能通过解析、却在含义上出错的回答。
oneSentenceSummary: 文章展示了如何通过语法模板进行受约束解码，确保小模型输出的 JSON 100% 有效，同时指出仅保证格式并不能避免那些仍能通过解析、却在含义上出错的回答。
summary: 本文探讨了如何使用语法模板进行受约束解码，确保一个小型语言模型（0.84M 参数）输出有效的 JSON。系统使用两种模板：目录模板用于保证结构正确，基于问题的模板则用于防止模型生成问题中未提及的值。对 2，000 个问题的测试显示，目录模板虽然实现了 100% 的 JSON 有效率，但完全匹配准确率仅从 47.3% 小幅提升至 50.5%。基于问题的模板则显著提升了完全匹配准确率，达到 71.3%，操作正确率达到 90.8%。关键在于，语法只能保证格式，不能保证含义；最危险的错误，是那些格式有效、语义却不正确的输出。文章强调，除了有效率，还应衡量「错误但有效」的输出。

mainPoints.point: 通过语法模板进行受约束解码，可确保小模型输出 100% 有效的 JSON
mainPoints.explanation: 在每一步生成时屏蔽无效词元，系统便能确保所有输出都符合预期的 JSON 结构，避免解析错误导致程序故障。

mainPoints.point: 格式保证无法阻止语义错误但结构有效的输出
mainPoints.explanation: 目录模板实现了 100% 的有效率，但完全匹配准确率仅从 47.3% 小幅提升至 50.5%。这说明有效的 JSON 仍可能包含错误的操作或参数，导致程序错误执行。

mainPoints.point: 将解码结果与问题内容核对的基于问题的解码，能显著提升准确率
mainPoints.explanation: 基于问题的模板阻止模型生成问题中未提及的值，使完全匹配准确率从 50.5% 提升至 71.3%，操作正确率则从 84.5% 提升至 90.8%。

mainPoints.point: 应重点监控的关键指标是「错误但有效」的输出，而不只是有效率
mainPoints.explanation: 程序会照常执行格式有效但内容错误的请求，因此这类不易察觉的失败比明显的解析错误更危险。基于问题的模板将错误但有效的输出比例从 49.5% 降至 28.7%。

keyQuotes: 语法能保证格式，却无法保证含义。
悄无声息的失败才是危险的。程序会毫不犹豫地执行一个有效却错误的请求。
所以，值得关注的指标是错误但有效的输出，而不是「输出有多常有效」。
受约束解码只需一个简短的函数，就能把格式从一种愿望变成保证。
